extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and attorneys appearing before the USPTO (respondents in OED disciplinary proceedings, counsel, and USPTO adjudicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used by the USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline and the adjudicating court for assessing practitioner misconduct in patent matters and for determining appropriate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must 'provide competent representation,' which 'requires the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence requires promptness, thoroughness, preparation, and attention to detail in the specific matter at hand. Prior successes or a large volume of past work (e.g., having obtained many patents) do not excuse failures of competence in a particular representation. Examples of competence failures include not monitoring the file or PAIR and making multiple mistakes that stem from lack of preparation. However, merely losing on the merits does not by itself establish a breach of competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must 'act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence includes timely responding to Office actions, checking for and addressing Notices (e.g., Notices of Abandonment, Notices of Publication), requesting extensions or paying required fees when needed, and generally staying abreast of developments. Neglecting to monitor PAIR or ignoring USPTO notices that lead to abandonment is a violation of diligence and competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner must '[k]eep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes forwarding significant Office communications (e.g., Notices of Publication, Notices of Abandonment, Final Office Actions), notifying clients of publication or abandonment and explaining practical consequences. Failing to forward notices, sending them by ineffective means (e.g., mail to an address the client does not use), or otherwise withholding status information can violate this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain matter sufficiently for informed decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner must explain the matter 'to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must explain Office actions, options for responding, consequences of publication/abandonment, costs (e.g., government fees), and the effect of forms (e.g., power of attorney or termination). Sending terse, unexplained communications or failing to obtain informed consent before filing substantive papers can violate this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptly comply with reasonable requests for information (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must '[p]romptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable requests include inquiries about case status, next steps, and how to view case records (Public/Private PAIR). Nonresponsive, evasive, or one-line inaccurate replies (e.g., 'Waiting on the patent office' when the application is abandoned) fail this requirement. Repeated failures to answer client information requests support a finding of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to consult and monitor PAIR as needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner is expected to consult PAIR as needed to respond to Office actions and avoid providing inaccurate information to the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While there is no requirement to check PAIR 'every five minutes,' reasonable promptness and diligence require staying abreast of the status of matters and checking PAIR when status is at issue or deadlines approach. Failure to check PAIR leading to missed deadlines, missed notices, or misinformation to the client is a competence/diligence violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely filing and procedural steps (extensions and fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to Office actions must be timely; practitioners should request extensions of time or pay late fees where appropriate to avoid abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a Response late without requesting an extension or paying required fees that results in abandonment is actionable neglect. Notices from USPTO that a filing was late must be acknowledged and addressed; ignoring such notices exacerbates misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forwarding notices and effective client notification
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must forward USPTO notices to clients in a timely and effective manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forwarding important notices (publication, abandonment) by appropriate and consistent means (e.g., email if that's the normal practice) and ensuring the client actually receives them is required. Sending a notice by mail to an address the client does not use, or otherwise attempting to conceal a notice, supports an inference of improper intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty; prohibition on conduct involving dishonesty, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are prohibited from engaging in 'conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dishonesty involves lack of truthfulness, straightforwardness, or trustworthiness. Misrepresentations to clients or USPTO can be sanctionable. However, to establish a §11.804(c) violation generally requires intent to deceive; negligent or mistaken misstatements without intent may not rise to this violation. Examples of dishonest conduct include intentionally misleading a client about whether a filing will wait for client input (when already filed) or taking steps to conceal an abandonment and misleading USPTO in a Petition to Revive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are prohibited from conduct that is 'prejudicial to the administration of justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that undermines public confidence in the legal profession or the legal system—such as dishonest behavior towards clients or the Office—meets this standard. Dishonesty toward a client that diminishes trust can therefore also violate §11.804(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Culpability levels: intentional, knowing, negligent (sanctioning consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing misconduct, the Court considers whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional or knowing misconduct carries greater culpability than negligence. A pattern of negligent behavior (e.g., failure to monitor cases) supports discipline for competence/diligence violations; intentional acts (e.g., deliberate concealment or misrepresentation) support more severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court determines violations based on 'clear and convincing evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings of violations of the Rules of Professional Conduct are made when supported by clear and convincing evidence. The Court weighs credibility of testimony (e.g., client statements) and corroborating documentation when applying this evidentiary standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO regulations require consideration of four factors when imposing sanctions: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court often looks to the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance in determining severity and whether aggravating/mitigating factors exist. Examples of aggravating factors include intentional concealment; mitigating factors may include lack of prior discipline or cooperative litigation posture. The extent of actual or potential harm (e.g., delay reducing patent term, client anxiety) influences sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ABA Standards as guidance in sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court commonly consults the American Bar Association's Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when determining proper length and severity of discipline and evaluating aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ABA Standards inform the proportionality of sanctions and help identify relevant aggravating/mitigating circumstances; they are used as guidance rather than as binding rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions and limits: losing merits not per se misconduct; single mistake vs pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Losing on the merits of a patent prosecution does not necessarily establish a breach of professional conduct; a single forgetful moment or honest mistake may not be actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court distinguishes between isolated errors and a pattern of neglect or intentional wrongdoing. Repeated failures to communicate, monitor, and meet deadlines create an evidentiary basis for finding violations; isolated typographical errors generally do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific examples of prohibited/culpable conduct (illustrative behaviors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative behaviors that the Court treats as misconduct include: filing a response a month late without extension or fee; failing to forward or meaningfully explain Notices of Publication/Abandonment; filing a Petition to Revive without client notification; misleading clients about filings or deadlines; and forwarding forms (e.g., power of attorney) without explaining effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete examples represent how the general rules apply in practice. The context (knowledge, timing, method of communication) determines whether the behavior is negligent or intentional and thus affects culpability and sanctioning.
